device.name: Instant Pot Smart Bluetooth (Smart-60)
device.notes:
The Instant Pot Smart (model Smart-60, 6 quart) was Instant Pot's first Bluetooth cooker. Its companion app, "Instant Pot Smart Cooker", is reported withdrawn from both app stores (OpenPot's README; no official notice was found) and owners report it stopped launching on iOS 14.5, and Instant Brands went through Chapter 11 in June 2023 before the appliance business re-emerged as Instant Pot Brands; nothing official drives these cookers any more. The cooker itself talks BLE straight to the phone with no account or cloud: 20-byte frames on a control characteristic start a program, and the cooker notifies its state, remaining time, pressure and temperature on another.
The phone must bond with the cooker first (hold Adjust about 3 s, then accept the operating system's pairing prompt), and only one phone can be connected at a time.

openness.notes: One open-source replacement app is the entire public record. Its README describes the protocol and its code implements a different, working version of several fields; this spec follows the code.

enter_pairing_mode.notes: The bond is accepted only after Adjust is held on the cooker, so a person has to be at the cooker to pair. The security mode is inferred: OpenPot calls the platform bond with no passkey handling and the manual mentions no code, so Just Works is assumed.

procedures.basis: Instant Pot Smart-60 user manual; OpenPot bonds before connecting.
procedures.name: Hold Adjust about 3 seconds

steps.action: While the phone is trying to pair, press and hold Adjust for about 3 seconds.
steps.expect: A short beep, then the phone's pairing prompt.

exclusivity.recovery: Disconnect the other phone or turn its Bluetooth off; the cooker serves one connection at a time.

unpair.clears: Every stored pairing at once; there is no per-phone removal on the cooker.

safety_advisory.detail: These commands start, change and cancel heating and pressure programs on a cooker the user may not be standing next to. A pressure cooker started empty, with the valve set wrong or with the lid off is a burn and scald hazard. A client should only offer start commands when the user confirms they are at the cooker, and should always offer Cancel. The cooker's own lid and pressure interlocks still apply; nothing here bypasses them.
safety_advisory.summary: Starting a pressure-cooking program remotely heats a sealed pot; never start one without someone at the cooker.

credentials.notes: No application-layer authentication beyond the BLE bond.
stored_on_device: Bluetooth bonds (more than one; the cooker counts them)
Clock, two delay-timer presets and the 12/24-hour setting

factory_reset.description: Two button holds in the Smart-60 manual touch the Bluetooth state: Pressure held for 10 seconds erases all pairings, and Adjust held for 10 seconds switches Bluetooth off or back on. A cooker that will not pair is usually one with Bluetooth switched off.
factory_reset.effect: The manual documents no full factory reset. The nearest thing erases every stored Bluetooth pairing, including the current phone's, and leaves cooking settings alone.

procedures.basis: Instant Pot Smart-60 user manual (Bluetooth section).
procedures.name: Erase all pairings

steps.action: Press and hold the Pressure button for 10 seconds.
steps.expect: A long beep; every phone has to pair again.

methods.description: Put the cooker into pairing with the Adjust button, bond from the phone, then connect, enable notifications on 0xdab2 and write commands to 0xdab1.
methods.name: Bond and connect

steps.action: With the cooker plugged in and Bluetooth on (the BT icon on the display), start a scan from the phone.
When the phone finds 'Instant Pot Smart', press and hold Adjust on the cooker for about 3 seconds until it beeps.
Accept the operating system's Bluetooth pairing prompt.
steps.expect: The phone icon on the cooker's display lights.

steps.action: Enable notifications on 0000dab2-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb and, optionally, write the current time to 0000daa1-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb.

setup.notes: No network provisioning: the cooker is BLE-only. The one-time step is a link-layer bond, started from the cooker's buttons; it is described in `pairing` and repeated in the method below so it reads in order.

rejoin.notes: No network membership. A new phone pairs alongside existing ones; the cooker keeps a count of paired devices.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project, and no captured frames from a cooker are published anywhere. The frames below are rendered from OpenPot's frame builders, so they prove the layout and checksum as OpenPot sends them, not that a cooker accepts every one.

evidence.documentation_review: OpenPot's README, TEMPERATURE.md and its BLE service and activity code were read on 2026-10-11, alongside the Smart-60 manual. No other public reverse-engineering of the cooker was found.
evidence.open_questions: Everything listed in remaining_unknowns: OpenPot's README and code disagree, and no captured frame from a real cooker has been published.

remaining_unknowns: Mode-byte values: README says f0 / b0 / 70; the code uses e0 / 60 / a0 plus 0x10 for high pressure. This spec follows the code.
Time fields: README says BCD; the code uses plain binary for cook time, delay, remaining time and timer presets. This spec follows the code.
Command byte offsets: README puts the delay at bytes 8-9 and the duration at 10; the code uses delay 7-8 and duration 9-10 (and one code path overwrites the mode byte with a delay, a bug).
Telemetry offsets: the README diagram is one byte off from the parser.
Program 0x06 is unassigned in both sources; Slow Cook is the likely missing program.
Characteristic properties come from the README, not a GATT dump; the pairing security mode is inferred.

cancel.description: Stop whatever program is running (program 0x0e, every other field zero).

keep_warm.description: Keep warm at Normal for 10 hours (program 0x0d, mode 0x40).

pressure_cook.description: Start Manual pressure cooking (program 0x0c) now, for a cook time in hours and minutes. Mode 0x30 is high pressure, 0x20 low. High pressure for 30 minutes renders as aa 55 5a 01 0c 20 30 00 00 00 1e 00 … 00 2c.

check.description: 0 minus the sum of bytes 0-18, mod 256; encoder-filled.

hours.description: Cook-time hours; the code caps pressure programs at 120 minutes.

start_program.advanced_reason: Raw program and mode bytes; the mode values are disputed between OpenPot's README and code.
start_program.description: Start any preset program now. Soup at Normal with high pressure for 30 minutes is program 0x0a, mode 0x70: aa 55 5a 01 0a 20 70 00 00 00 1e 00 … 00 ee. Rice takes no time (send 0 and 0). See the service notes for which mode bytes each program family takes.

check.description: 0 minus the sum of bytes 0-18, mod 256; encoder-filled.

mode.description: Mode-flag byte; see the service notes. Unverified on hardware.

characteristics.name: Command
characteristics.notes: OpenPot writes without response. 20-byte command frames; see the service notes for the layout.

format.name: work_state
format.notes: Any other value means off / standby.

format.name: temperature_raw
format.notes: Raw sensor count; map through OpenPot's TEMPERATURE.md table. Not linear.

format.name: heating_level
format.notes: 0-16; percent of full heat is value / 16 x 100.

characteristics.name: Status
characteristics.notes: 20-byte status frames starting aa 55 40 02 (OpenPot checks only byte 2 = 0x40). Offsets are the ones OpenPot's parser uses; the README's diagram is one byte off from them. Temperature is a raw sensor count, converted to degrees through a non-linear table that OpenPot publishes in TEMPERATURE.md (about 25 C at 24, 104 C at 153, saturating at 210 C from 243); it is cited rather than copied.

services.name: Cooker control service
services.notes:
Command frames go to 0xdab1, state comes back on 0xdab2. Every frame in both directions is 20 bytes, and its last byte makes the sum of all 20 bytes 0 modulo 256 (the two's complement of the sum of bytes 0-18). Commands start aa 55 5a 01; telemetry starts aa 55 40 02.
COMMAND LAYOUT (OpenPot's code): byte 4 program, byte 5 start mode (0x20 now, 0x11 after delay timer 1, 0x12 after delay timer 2), byte 6 mode flags, bytes 7-8 delay hours and minutes, bytes 9-10 cook hours and minutes, bytes 11-18 zero, byte 19 check. Times are plain binary in the code (30 minutes is 0x1e); OpenPot's README says BCD.
MODE BYTE (byte 6), as the code builds it: bits 7-6 select Less (11), Normal (01) or More (10), 00 when not applicable; bit 5 marks a pressure program; bit 4 selects high pressure. So pressure programs use 0xe0 / 0x60 / 0xa0 for less / normal / more, plus 0x10 for high pressure; Manual and Rice use 0x30 (high) or 0x20 (low); Keep Warm and Sauté use 0xc0 / 0x40 / 0x80; Yogurt uses 0xc0 pasteurise, 0x40 yogurt, 0x80 ferment. The README gives different values (f0 / b0 / 70) and the code's own comment disagrees with the code.

characteristics.name: Clock
characteristics.notes: Seconds since 2001-01-01 00:00:00 LOCAL time (no time zone), as a 32-bit LITTLE-endian integer. OpenPot's README says big-endian, but its own example only decodes little-endian and its code writes little-endian. 2024-10-17 12:00:00 encodes as c0 33 c1 2c.

characteristics.name: Delay timer 1 preset
characteristics.notes: Two bytes, hours then minutes (plain binary in the code; README says BCD).

characteristics.name: 12/24-hour display
characteristics.notes: One byte; which value means 24-hour is inconsistent even inside OpenPot's code.

services.name: Clock and timers service
services.notes: Characteristic properties are from OpenPot's README, not a GATT dump; OpenPot writes each without response.

services.name: Recipe service
services.notes: One write characteristic taking multi-step recipe scripts in the same 20-byte framing, described only in OpenPot's README (OpenPot never implemented it). Not specified further here.
